title: Programming & Control
blurb: From dataflow logic to live control.

topics.name: Dataflow Paradigm
topics.question: Why does LabVIEW not run top-to-bottom
topics.assetAlt: Example data-flow diagram of an online purchase: labelled arrows carry data between customer, shopping cart, checkout, payment, accounting and inventory nodes, so each process can run only once its input data has arrived.
topics.summary: Execution by data availability.

sections.heading: Execution by data, not lines
paragraphs: In a dataflow language a node executes the moment all its inputs are available — not in textual order. Independent branches run in parallel automatically, which is powerful but surprising if you think sequentially.

sections.heading: Forcing order
paragraphs: When order matters (open port → read → close), you create artificial data dependencies — error clusters wired in series, or a Sequence structure — so one node cannot start until the previous finishes.

topics.hint: A LabVIEW VI running its steps in the "wrong" order has no implied sequence — chain the error in/out wire through the nodes, or wrap them in a Flat Sequence, to force order.

topics.name: LabVIEW Loops
topics.question: How do I use loops and shift registers in LabVIEW
topics.assetAlt: Screenshot of a large LabVIEW block diagram: nested while loops and case structures joined by coloured wires that carry data between string, numeric and Boolean terminals, subVIs and indicators.
topics.summary: Repeating logic and remembering state.

sections.heading: Front panel + block diagram
paragraphs: Every VI has a front panel (the UI) and a block diagram (the graphical code). You build behaviour by wiring nodes; While and For loops repeat a section of diagram.

sections.heading: Shift registers
paragraphs: A plain wire inside a loop resets every iteration. A shift register carries a value from one iteration to the next — essential for running totals, filters and state machines.

topics.hint: A value that resets to its default every loop iteration was wired through a tunnel — right-click the loop border and Replace with Shift Register to persist it.

topics.name: LabVIEW LINX
topics.question: How do I drive Arduino pins from LabVIEW with LINX
topics.assetAlt: Screenshot of the LabVIEW MakerHub functions palette expanded to show the LINX sub-palette (Open, Close, Peripherals, Sensors, Utilities) and the Toolbox sub-palette.
topics.summary: Controlling Arduino from the diagram.

sections.heading: What LINX does
paragraphs: The LINX (Hobbyist) toolkit lets LabVIEW read and write Arduino pins directly — analog read, digital write, PWM — without writing C. Deploy its firmware once, then drive the board from the block diagram.

sections.heading: Session management
paragraphs: Open the LINX session once before your main loop and close it once after — never inside the loop. Match the baud rate and select the correct COM port.

topics.hint: LINX that runs slowly or errors repeatedly is opening/closing the session inside the loop — open before the loop, pass the reference through a shift register, close after.

topics.name: LabVIEW VISA
topics.question: How do I read an Arduino serial stream with VISA
topics.assetAlt: LabVIEW block diagram for VISA serial input: a COM-port control and 9600-baud constant configure the serial port, a while loop polls Bytes at Port and reads into a string indicator, and VISA Close runs after the stop button.
topics.summary: Parsing raw serial in LabVIEW.

sections.heading: When to use VISA
paragraphs: When you write your own Arduino sketch that prints over Serial, VISA is how LabVIEW reads that stream. Configure the port (baud, data bits), then read/write bytes and parse them.

sections.heading: Framing the data
paragraphs: Agree on a termination character (usually newline) on both sides so VISA knows where one message ends, and configure the serial read to stop on that terminator.

topics.hint: VISA returning garbage, partial lines, or hanging is nearly always a baud-rate or termination-character mismatch — set both ends identical and clear the buffer before reading.

topics.name: Threshold Control
topics.question: How do I turn a sensor reading into an action on the Arduino
topics.assetAlt: Arduino threshold sketch listing: constants set the sensor pin A0, the LED pin and a threshold of 500; setup() configures the pins and serial port; loop() reads the sensor, prints the value, and drives the LED HIGH below the threshold and LOW otherwise.
topics.summary: analogRead → if/else → digitalWrite.

sections.heading: Read, compare, act
paragraphs: In `loop()`, read the sensor with `analogRead()`, compare it to a threshold with an `if/else`, and command an actuator with `digitalWrite()`. This is the automatic-lighting pattern at the heart of the labs.

sections.heading: Choosing the threshold
paragraphs: Set the threshold from calibrated measurements, and test around the boundary — not just obvious cases — so the actuator switches cleanly rather than chattering near the limit.

topics.hint: An actuator that chatters on and off near the trigger point needs hysteresis — use two thresholds (one to turn on, a separate one to turn off) instead of a single value.

topics.summary: Repeat LabVIEW calculations or measurements while the interface remains responsive, then stop through a defined condition.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: A While Loop repeatedly runs the code inside its border. In a LabVIEW VI, this lets indicators update as controls or measurements change and keeps the front panel responsive until the wired Stop condition becomes true.

sections.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs: Used in Lab 1, Lab 2, Lab 4, Lab 5, Lab 6, Lab 7, Lab 8. Prerequisites: block-diagram.

topics.hint: Place the calculation or measurement inside the loop, wire a front-panel Stop control to the loop condition, and use that control instead of repeatedly pressing Run or stopping with Abort.

topics.name: Data Types, Arrays, and Clusters
topics.question: What do LabVIEW wires carry, and when do values belong in an array or a cluster
topics.summary: What LabVIEW wire types carry and when to group values into arrays or clusters.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: Numeric wires carry numbers, Boolean wires carry true or false, and strings carry text. Arrays hold multiple values of one type. Clusters group related values and may combine different types.

topics.hint: Five voltage readings naturally form an array; a student ID plus readings plus a completion flag could form a cluster.

topics.name: While Loops, For Loops, and Shift Registers
topics.question: When do you repeat with a while loop or a for loop, and how does state carry between iterations
topics.summary: Choosing between while and for loops, and carrying values across iterations.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: A while loop repeats until a stop condition is met. A for loop repeats a known number of times. A shift register carries a value from one iteration to the next.

topics.hint: The LabVIEW exercise uses a while loop so the calculation can continue until the user stops it.

topics.name: Analog Input and Digital Output
topics.question: How does an analog input reading become a digital output command
topics.summary: Reading a range of voltages on an analog pin and commanding an output LOW or HIGH.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: Analog input A0 reads a range of voltages as a number. Digital pin 7 commands the LED as LOW or HIGH.

topics.hint: Use A0 for the sensor voltage and D7 for the LED state.

topics.name: Arduino Code Flow
topics.question: How does an Arduino sketch flow from `setup()` through the repeating `loop()`
topics.summary: How a sketch’s setup, loop, reads, writes, and branches fit together.

sections.heading: Core idea
paragraphs: `setup()` runs once. `loop()` repeats continuously. `analogRead()` samples the sensor. `digitalWrite()` controls the output. `if/else` selects the LED action.

topics.hint: If PR is below `lowLightLim`, the given code writes HIGH to `LEDPin`.
